headline: PAGASA: Offshore LPA Has High Chance of Becoming Tropical Depression
kicker: Weather update · Philippine Sea · Southwest monsoon
deck: PAGASA said a low pressure area far east of Northern Luzon had a high chance of becoming a tropical depression, while assessing a low chance that it would enter PAR or directly affect the country.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: PAGASA said on Saturday morning, August 8, that a low pressure area outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility had a high chance of developing into a tropical depression within 24 hours.

sections.heading: What we know
paragraphs: The weather disturbance was estimated at 2,610 kilometers east of Northern Luzon at 3:00 a.m. PAGASA weather specialist Veronica Torres said it had a low chance of directly affecting the country and a low chance of entering PAR.

PAGASA was also monitoring Typhoon Dolphin outside PAR. At 3:00 a.m., Dolphin was 810 kilometers northeast of Extreme Northern Luzon, with maximum sustained winds of 155 kilometers per hour and gusts of up to 190 kilometers per hour, moving southwest at 15 kilometers per hour.

Dolphin continued to enhance the southwest monsoon over Luzon and the Visayas. PAGASA forecast monsoon rains over Occidental Mindoro, Zambales, and Bataan and occasional rains over Metro Manila and several other parts of Luzon and Antique.

sections.heading: Background
paragraphs: Tropical cyclones and low pressure areas outside PAR can strengthen the southwest monsoon even when they are unlikely to cross the country's monitoring boundary or make landfall. Their indirect effect can still bring prolonged rain, rough seas, flash floods, and landslides.

sections.heading: What remains unclear
paragraphs: The low pressure area's development and track may change. PAGASA's morning assessment indicated a low chance of entry into PAR or a direct effect on the Philippines, but the bureau will continue monitoring it.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Even a distant weather system can influence rainfall and sea conditions through the southwest monsoon. Communities in rain-affected areas should follow official flood, landslide, coastal, and local-government advisories rather than treating distance from PAR as an absence of risk.

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: PAGASA will continue updating the public on the low pressure area, Typhoon Dolphin, the southwest monsoon, and any changes in rainfall or coastal hazards.
